before: EGEON. A heavier task could not have been imposed on me than to speak my unspeakable griefs. Still, so the world may witness that my end was caused by fate, not by any vile crime, I'll tell what my sorrow allows me to say. I was born in Syracuse, and married to a woman who would have been happy — except for me, and through no fault but our bad luck. I lived with her in joy. Our wealth grew through the successful voyages I often made to Epidamnum, until my agent there died and the great burden of unmanaged goods drew me away from my wife's embrace. I had not been gone six months before she — almost ready to faint under the pleasant burden women bear — made arrangements to follow me, and soon arrived safely where I was. She had not been there long before she became the joyful mother of two fine sons, and — strangely — one looked so like the other that they could be told apart only by their names. In that very same hour, and at the same inn, a poor woman gave birth to a similar pair, male twins, also identical. Because their parents were extremely poor, I bought them and raised them to wait on my sons. My wife, not a little proud of two such boys, asked daily that we go home. Reluctantly, I agreed; alas, too soon. We had sailed only a league from Epidamnum before the always-obedient sea gave any tragic sign of our coming disaster. But we soon lost much hope, for what little light the heavens granted only brought to our terrified minds a near-certain warning of immediate death — which I myself would gladly have embraced, but the constant weeping of my wife, weeping in anticipation of what she saw coming, and the pitiful crying of the pretty babies, who cried because that's what they saw us doing without knowing what to fear, forced me to find delays for them and for myself. And it came to this — for there was no other option. The sailors took the lifeboat to save themselves, leaving us the ship, which was on the verge of sinking. My wife, more concerned for the younger-born, had tied him to a small spare mast, the kind sailors keep on board for storms. One of the other twins was bound to him, while I had done the same with the other pair. With the children thus secured, my wife and I, keeping our eyes fixed on the children we cared for, tied ourselves to either end of the mast, and floating along, carried by the current, were swept towards Corinth, as we thought. At last the sun, gazing on the earth, dispersed those threatening clouds, and by the help of its welcome light the seas grew calm. We spotted two ships in the distance, racing toward us — one from Corinth, the other from Epidaurus. But before they reached us — oh, let me say no more! Guess the rest from what came before.
after: EGEON. A heavier task could not have been imposed on me than to speak my unspeakable griefs. Still, so the world may witness that my end came from my love for my family, not by any vile crime, I'll tell what my sorrow allows me to say. I was born in Syracuse, and married to a woman who would have been happy without me, and happy with me too if our luck had held. I lived with her in joy. Our wealth grew through the successful voyages I often made to Epidamnum, until my agent there died and the great burden of unmanaged goods drew me away from my wife's embrace. before: EGEON. Oh, had the gods done so, I would not now rightly call them merciless to us. For before the ships could close to within ten leagues, we crashed into a mighty rock, and as we were violently thrown against it our rescue-ship was split down the middle. So that, in this cruel separation, Fortune had left each of us an equal share of joy and grief. My wife's portion — poor soul — appeared burdened with less weight, but not less sorrow. She was carried more swiftly before the wind, and we saw the three of them picked up by fishermen of Corinth, as we believed. At length another ship caught up with us; and knowing whose lives they had the luck to save, they gave us a warm welcome aboard, and would have taken the prize from the fishermen, had their boat not been very slow under sail. So instead they turned and headed home. Thus you have heard how I was cut off from my happiness, my life prolonged by misfortune only to tell sad stories of my own disasters.
after: EGEON. Oh, had the gods done so, I would not now rightly call them merciless to us. For before the ships could close to within ten leagues, we crashed into a mighty rock, and as we were violently thrown against it the spare mast that kept us afloat was split down the middle. So that, in this cruel separation, Fortune had left each of us an equal share of joy and grief. My wife's portion — poor soul — appeared burdened with less weight, but not less sorrow. She was carried more swiftly before the wind, and we saw the three of them picked up by fishermen of Corinth, as we believed. At length another ship caught up with us; and knowing whose lives they had the luck to save, they gave us a warm welcome aboard, and would have taken the prize from the fishermen, had their boat not been very slow under sail. So instead they turned and headed home. Thus you have heard how I was cut off from my happiness, my life prolonged by misfortune only to tell sad stories of my own disasters.

before: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Many a man would take you at your word and actually leave, with such a good opportunity.
after: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Many a man would take you at your word and really go, with the means to do it in his hand.

before: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Please save the jokes for when you're sitting at dinner, sir. I've come to you in a rush from my mistress. If I go back empty-handed, I'll be a post indeed, for she'll chalk up your fault on my skull. It seems to me your stomach, like mine, should be your clock, and strike you homeward without need of a messenger.
after: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Save your jokes for dinner, sir. My mistress sent me here posthaste. If I go back without you, I'll be a post for her to notch your faults on, right across my skull. Your stomach should be as good a clock as mine and strike you home without a messenger.

before: ADRIANA. But if you were married, you'd want some control.
after: ADRIANA. But if you were married, you'd have some say yourself.

before: LUCIANA. Well, I'll marry one day, just to try it. Here's your man — your husband must be near.
after: LUCIANA. Well, I'll marry one day just to try it. Here comes your servant. Your husband must be nearby.

before: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. No, he's at fists with me — and my two ears can vouch for it.
after: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. At hand? He's been at me with both hands, and my two ears can testify to it.

before: ADRIANA. Get back, slave, or I'll crack open your skull.
after: ADRIANA. Get back there, slave, or I'll split your skull crosswise!

before: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. And he'll bless that crack with another beating. Between the two of you, I'll have a holy head.
after: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Then he'll bless that cross with another beating. Between you I'll have a holy head.

before: ADRIANA. His company must be making his mistresses happy, while I starve at home for one cheerful look from him. Has homely old age stolen the alluring beauty from my poor cheeks? Then he's worn it out. Is my conversation dull? My wit barren? If lively, sharp talk is ruined in me, his unkindness has blunted it harder than marble. Do their fancy clothes bait his affections? That's not my fault — he controls my wardrobe. What is ruined in me that wasn't ruined by him? Then he is the cause of my decay. One sunny look from him would soon repair my withered beauty. But the unruly deer breaks the fence and feeds away from home; poor me, I'm only his stale leftover.
after: ADRIANA. His company must be making his mistresses happy, while I starve at home for one cheerful look from him. Has homely old age stolen the alluring beauty from my poor cheeks? Then he's worn it out. Is my conversation dull? My wit barren? If lively, sharp talk is ruined in me, his unkindness has blunted it harder than marble. Do their fancy clothes bait his affections? That's not my fault — he controls my means. What is ruined in me that wasn't ruined by him? Then he is the cause of my decay. One sunny look from him would soon repair my withered beauty. But the unruly deer breaks the fence and feeds away from home; poor me, I'm only his stale leftover.

before: ADRIANA. Only the unfeeling can shrug off wrongs like these. I know his eye is paying respects elsewhere — what else could be keeping him away from here? Sister, you know he promised me a chain. I'd give up that gift, even a portion of his love, if only he'd keep faith with our bed. I see that even the most beautifully enamelled jewel loses its beauty in time; yet the gold underneath endures even what others touch — though frequent touching will wear gold thin. And no man with a good name shames it through dishonesty and corruption — and yet so it goes. Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep what's left of it away, and weeping, die.
after: ADRIANA. Only the unfeeling can shrug off wrongs like these. I know his eye is paying respects elsewhere — what else could be keeping him away from here? Sister, you know he promised me a chain. If only that chain were the one token of love he kept from me, and he'd keep faith with our bed. I see that even the most beautifully enamelled jewel loses its beauty in time; yet the gold underneath endures even what others touch — though frequent touching will wear gold thin. And no man with a good name shames it through dishonesty and corruption — and yet so it goes. Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep what's left of it away, and weeping, die.

before: LUCIANA. How many doting fools jealousy drives to madness!
after: LUCIANA. How many lovesick fools are slaves to mad jealousy!

before: ADRIANA. How poorly it suits your seriousness to play along so crudely with your slave, encouraging him to thwart me in my mood. Whatever wrong I've done you, you don't have to add to that wrong with more contempt. Come, I'll cling to this sleeve of yours. You are an elm, my husband; I, a vine, whose weakness, married to your stronger frame, shares in your strength. If anything pulls you away from me, it's rubbish — usurping ivy, briar, or idle moss — which, for lack of pruning, all push in to infect your sap, and live off your decline.
after: ADRIANA. How poorly it suits your seriousness to play along so crudely with your slave, encouraging him to thwart me in my mood. You stay away from me, and that hurts me. Don't add contempt to the wrong. Come, I'll cling to this sleeve of yours. You are an elm, my husband; I, a vine, whose weakness, married to your stronger frame, shares in your strength. If anything pulls you away from me, it's rubbish — usurping ivy, briar, or idle moss — which, for lack of pruning, all push in to infect your sap, and live off your decline.

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. She's speaking to me; she's making me her subject. What, did I marry her in a dream? Or am I sleeping now and only think I hear this? What error has my eyes and ears so wrong? Until I'm sure about this strange uncertainty, I'll play along with the fantasy being offered.
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. She's speaking to me; I'm the subject of her speech. What, did I marry her in a dream? Or am I sleeping now and only think I hear this? What error has my eyes and ears so wrong? Until I'm sure about this strange uncertainty, I'll play along with the fantasy being offered.

before: LUCE. I thought I was the one to be asked.
after: LUCE. That's what I meant to ask you!

before: BALTHASAR. While we debate which is better, we'll part with neither.
after: BALTHASAR. While we've been debating which was better, it seems we're going away with neither.

before: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, such a claim as you'd lay on your horse — she'd have me as a beast. Not because, being a beast, she'd have me — but because, being a very beastly creature, she lays claim to me.
after: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. The same claim you'd lay on your horse, sir. She wants me as her beast. It's not that I'm a beast and that's why she wants me. She's the beastly creature for laying claim to me.

before: MERCHANT. My business can't tolerate this delay. Good sir, tell me: will you answer me or not? If not, I'll leave him to the officer.
after: MERCHANT. My business won't wait for this fooling around. Are you going to answer for the debt or not, sir? Otherwise I'll leave him to the officer.

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I answer you? What should I answer you?
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Me, answer you? What have I got to answer for?

before: ADRIANA. He means he gave me none — that's worse for me.
after: ADRIANA. He means he didn't do right by me. All the more wrong I've suffered!

before: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, he's in a Tartar limbo, worse than hell. A devil in an everlasting coat has hold of him — one whose hard heart is buttoned up with steel; a fiend, a fairy, pitiless and rough; a wolf — no, worse — a fellow all in buff leather; a back-stabbing friend, a shoulder-tapper, one who blocks the passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lanes; a hound that runs the wrong way and yet hunts well by scent; one who, before the judgement, carries poor souls to hell.
after: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, he's in the limbo of Tartarus, worse than hell. A devil in a coat that never wears out has him. His hard heart is buttoned up with steel. A fiend, a spiteful fairy, pitiless and rough. A wolf? Worse, a fellow all in buff leather! A friend who takes you from behind and claps you on the shoulder. He blocks alleys, creeks and narrow ways. A hound that runs the trail backward yet tracks a man on dry ground. He takes poor souls to hell before they're even judged.

before: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, if you do, expect baby food — or ask for a long spoon.
after: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, if you go, expect something you eat with a spoon. Better ask for a long one!

before: PINCH. It's not a shame; the fellow finds his pattern, and by going along with him, he soothes his frenzy well.
after: PINCH. There's no harm in it. He's found the pitch of his master's mood, and by playing along he does a good job of calming him.

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Tell me, why did you lock me out today? And why do you deny sending the bag of gold?
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Tell me, why did you lock me out today? And why did you refuse me the bag of gold?

before: ADRIANA. He ordered a chain for me, but never gave it to me.
after: ADRIANA. He ordered a chain for me, but he never got it.

before: MESSENGER. O mistress, mistress, save yourself and flee! My master and his man are both broken loose, beaten the maids one after another, and bound the doctor, whose beard they've singed off with flaming brands, and as it blazed they kept throwing on him great pails of muddy water to quench the hair. My master preaches patience to him, while his man, with scissors, snips at him like a fool. And I'm sure (unless you send some immediate help) between them they will kill the conjurer.
after: MESSENGER. Mistress, mistress, run and save yourself! My master and his servant have both broken loose. They've beaten the maids one after another and tied up the doctor. They set his beard alight with flaming brands and kept tossing buckets of muddy water over him to put it out. My master preaches patience to him while the servant clips his hair with scissors to make him look like a court fool. Unless you send help right now, the pair of them will kill the conjurer!

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Justice, most gracious Duke! Oh, grant me justice! Even for the service I once did you, when I rode beside you in the wars, and took deep wounds to save your life — even for the blood I lost for you then — now grant me justice.
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Justice, gracious Duke! Grant me justice! Remember what I did for you in battle, when I stood over you to shield you and took deep wounds to save your life. For the blood I lost for you then, grant me justice now.

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Today, great Duke, she shut the doors against me while she feasted in my house with harlots.
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Today, great Duke, she shut me out while she feasted with a pack of scoundrels in my own house.

before: EGEON. Oh, grief has changed me since you saw me last, and careful hours, with time's deformed hand, have written strange ravages on my face. But tell me yet — don't you recognize my voice?
after: EGEON. Grief has changed me since you last saw me. Hours full of worry and the disfiguring hand of time have written strange lines across my face. But tell me, don't you recognize my voice?

before: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. There, take it — and many thanks for my entertainment.
after: ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Here, take it, and many thanks for your hospitality.

before: ABBESS. Renowned Duke, take the trouble to come with us into the abbey here, and hear at length all our fortunes recounted. And all who are gathered in this place, who through this sympathetic single day's confusion have suffered wrong, come, keep us company, and we'll make full restitution. Thirty-three years have I been in labour with you, my sons — and till this hour my heavy burden never delivered. The Duke, my husband, and both my children, and you, the calendars of their birth, come to a christening feast, and come with me. After such long grief, such a nativity.
after: ABBESS. Renowned Duke, please come with us into the abbey here, and hear at length all our fortunes recounted. And all who are gathered in this place, who through the confusion we've all shared this one day have suffered wrong, come, keep us company, and we'll make full restitution. Thirty-three years have I been in labour with you, my sons — and till this hour my heavy burden never delivered. The Duke, my husband, and both my children, and you, the calendars of their birth, come to a christening feast, and come with me. After such long grief, such a nativity.

before: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I think you're my mirror, not my brother. I see by you that I'm a sweet-faced youth. Will you come in to watch their christening?
after: DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I think you're my mirror instead of my brother. Looking at you, I see what a sweet-faced young fellow I am. Shall we go in and see them celebrating?
